title: The Kids Wrote the Policy This Summer. Adults Need to Execute
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Andrew Marcinek describes how ninety-eight high school students, roughly two per state, passed a model K-12 AI policy called the Students First Act at a mock Senate in Boston, and argues that districts should answer it provision by provision. The students asked for AI literacy from the day a device arrives, AI kept out of their writing until after eighth grade, teacher permission before use, verification of mastery when AI touches a draft, transparency about data collection, and chatbots that decline to act as emotional support. Marcinek contrasts this with the dominant adult response of bans, such as New York City's moratorium, and cites survey data showing that most teens use AI for schoolwork, most have never been taught to use it safely, and many simply move to a personal device when blocked. His practical advice is to seat two or three students with real work, including one daily user and one refuser, and to answer each provision with yes and a date, no and a reason, or not yet and what would change their mind.
points: Restriction without teaching pushes use onto personal phones, so the real data lives in the space between blocking tools and teaching students.
The students' bill is mostly executable this year without purchases: literacy scheduled with devices, a syllabus paragraph on permission, and a defined way to verify mastery.
Genuine consultation is the step districts most often skip, and the test is whether a sentence in the draft changed because of student input.
Student seats on a committee need defined roles, such as redesigning assignments, beta-testing tools, and joining procurement, or they become tokenistic.
Leaders should answer every provision in writing with yes and a date, no and a reason, or not yet and what would change their mind.
quotes: The test of whether anyone listened is whether a sentence in the district’s draft changed because of theirs.
Securing a temporary pause remains a pragmatic move for any district, yet halting progress hardly equates to strategy.
The tool vanishes from the filter logs and reappears on a phone under the desk, where no one is teaching anything.
Seven in ten teens use AI for schoolwork, and seventy-three percent say no teacher has ever talked with them about how to use it safely, which as far as I’m concerned is the whole argument.
Put one kid on it who uses AI every day and one who refuses to touch it, because the policy has to survive both. Give them real work rather than a listening session.
Agency, the panel agreed, is when the seat changes what the district does.
Listening is the cheaper half. Where I’d push school leaders hardest is on executing, because the students’ bill is unusual in that almost all of it can be done this year without buying anything.
